title: Greece Locks In a $4B US Arms Package as a Congressional Report Puts the Iran War's Aircraft Bill at $3.3B
subhead: Athens signs up to F-16 Viper upgrades, F-35 munitions and Strykers right after Rubio's Strategic Dialogue visit, while a new congressional tally nearly doubles the count of lost or damaged US aircraft — a reminder that the airpower bill for this war keeps growing.

sections.heading: Greece Commits Up to $4 Billion in US Weapons After Rubio Visit
sections.body:
Greece has agreed to spend as much as $4 billion on US weapons and aircraft upgrades, two senior sources told Reuters, finalized in the wake of the sixth round of the US-Greece Strategic Dialogue in Athens on Oct. 7, co-chaired by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis. A senior Greek defense ministry official told Reuters/IBTimes the package includes advanced missiles and precision-guided bombs for Greece's F-16 Viper and F-35 fighters and its Black Hawk helicopters, plus the upgrade of 37 F-16 Block 50s to the Viper configuration. The joint statement also confirmed the provision of Stryker armored vehicles, though the statement left unclear whether the Strykers are inside the $4 billion figure.

The purchases run through the Foreign Military Sales program, with Greek officials saying most were already budgeted in the country's multiyear defense plan and spending will be spread over several years. Athens has an estimated 28 billion euros in planned defense spending through 2036, covering F-35s, helicopters and the Israeli-equipped 'Achilles Shield' layered air-defense system. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in July that Greece had reached NATO's 3.5% defense-spending target for 2026.
sections.whyItMatters: Greece is converting its NATO spending commitment directly into US-sourced capability, deepening a supplier relationship that doubles as its counterweight to Turkey. The Stryker element is notable: it moves Athens beyond air power into land systems interoperability with US formations. Every one of these deals also locks Greece further into the US FMS pipeline rather than European alternatives.

sections.heading: Pentagon Hands Raytheon a $6.3B Multi-Year SM-3 Interceptor Contract
sections.body: The Pentagon awarded RTX's Raytheon a multi-year contract worth up to $6.3 billion to produce SM-3 Block IB interceptor missiles, Breaking Defense and MarketWatch reported. The base term runs five years with an option for two more. MarketWatch notes Raytheon will build the interceptors under the grant. Breaking Defense notes the deal comes months after the Department of Defense and Raytheon inked a framework agreement intended to boost production of the air-defense munition.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the interceptor layer of the same demand surge that produced the earlier SM-6 awards — the US is trying to convert framework agreements into actual production contracts. SM-3 is the ship-based ballistic-missile defense backbone for both US Navy Aegis ships and allied navies, so the multi-year structure is a bet that demand from Europe, the Gulf and the Indo-Pacific will hold. The option years signal the Pentagon expects the threat picture to keep worsening, not stabilize.

sections.heading: South Korea Test-Fires Its First Domestically Built Hypersonic Glide Vehicle
sections.body:
President Lee Jae-myung personally observed the first test launch of a domestically developed hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) on Oct. 8, according to the presidential office via Yonhap and Sedaily. The test took place at the Agency for Defense Development's Anheung test center in Taean. Senior spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said the HGV climbed to altitude, separated from its booster, performed 'irregular gliding flight' at low altitude — changing trajectory vertically and horizontally — and struck its designated target point. The vehicle is designed to fly at Mach 5 or faster. The stated purpose was to verify ultra-high-temperature heat-resistant materials, guidance and control, and low-altitude irregular flight.

The office framed the milestone as a step toward 'a new deterrent capable of striking key targets in the Korean Peninsula battlefield environment.' The test follows a run of North Korean hypersonic missile launches overseen by Kim Jong-un.
sections.whyItMatters: Seoul is signaling that it will not simply buy its way into the hypersonics club — it wants domestic design and production, which builds an industrial base that can later feed exports. The timing is a direct answer to Pyongyang's hypersonic demonstrations: South Korea is matching capability with capability rather than relying on US umbrella coverage alone. The verification of heat-resistant materials is the hard technical bottleneck, so a successful glide is a genuine engineering milestone.

sections.heading: Congressional Report Nearly Doubles the Tally of US Aircraft Lost or Damaged in the Iran War
sections.body: A new congressional report says the US has lost or sustained damage to 81 military aircraft worth up to $3.3 billion in the Iran war, per MSN/CBS coverage of the findings. That is almost double the 42 aircraft the same non-partisan agency counted six months earlier. An F-35A is among the losses. Separately, Forbes (William Hartung) argues the full costs of the war are becoming clearer by the day.
sections.whyItMatters: The revised count matters less as a battlefield scorecard than as a procurement signal. Doubling the count of damaged or lost airframes in six months implies a steady stream of attrition replacement demand — new airframes, repair capacity and munitions restocking — on top of a wartime production surge already stretching US lines. It also undercuts the assumption that high-end stealth aircraft are cheap to operate in a contested environment.

sections.heading: UK Think Tank: Britain's Military Is Over-Invested Overseas, and More Money Will Just Be Wasted
sections.body:
A report by researchers at the Transition Security Project warns that the UK's military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defense, meaning the government's planned spending increase risks producing 'even greater waste,' according to The Guardian. Using 2024-25 figures, the study estimates about 23% of the military budget — just over 14 billion pounds — went to overseas commitments, with roughly 2.8 billion pounds on force-projection deployments including bases in Cyprus, Kenya and Oman. It calls the UK the most overseas-committed military among European NATO members.

The report lands as the government targets 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, which the study says implies a nominal doubling from 70 billion pounds in 2026 to 151 billion in 2035. It notes that a 3% by 2030 target championed by former defense secretary John Healey — now chancellor — has been shelved. The Transition Security Project is a research center spun out of Common Wealth, a think tank with links to PM Andy Burnham.
sections.whyItMatters: This is an argument about where the money goes, not how much — a live fight inside European rearmament. If domestic-first thinking gains traction, it shifts procurement toward homeland air defense, munitions stockpiles and industrial capacity rather than expeditionary enablers. For suppliers, that changes what gets ordered and where the political pressure lands.

sections.heading: Burnham Invites Germany to Join the GCAP Fighter Program
sections.body: On his first Berlin visit as prime minister, UK PM Andy Burnham told Chancellor Friedrich Merz that Britain is open to Germany joining GCAP, the UK-Italy-Japan sixth-generation fighter program, according to the Japan Times and Firstpost. The move comes amid mounting speculation that GCAP could open its doors to Germany, especially after difficulties in the rival Franco-German FCAS program. Burnham framed the invitation as part of bringing the UK closer to Europe.
sections.whyItMatters: If Germany swings from FCAS toward GCAP, it would reorder Europe's two competing sixth-generation fighter efforts and hand the UK-led program the industrial and financial weight of Europe's largest economy. It also has export consequences: a bigger GCAP consortium means a larger built-in market and a stronger position against US and future Chinese platforms. The FCAS side of this equation is the one to watch next.

sections.heading: Dutch AI Firm Links Disparate Air-Defense Systems on Ukraine's Battlefield
sections.body: Dutch company Intelic has built an AI-based system that lets air-defense systems and radars 'talk' to one another, integrating different equipment into a single network for Ukraine's Defense Forces, Reuters reported. The aim is faster, more coordinated response to Russian drone and missile attacks. The work sits alongside a broader effort: the US is helping Ukraine repair Patriot air-defense systems domestically as Russian missile attacks intensify, per Army Recognition, and Germany is supplying weapons to counter jet-powered drones, per Ukrainian media. Ukraine's cities are facing a documented shortfall in air defense, per Reuters commentary.
sections.whyItMatters: Software that fuses mismatched sensors and shooters is becoming as decisive as the interceptors themselves, because Ukraine fields a patchwork of Western and Soviet-era systems. If Intelic's approach scales, it points to a template — and a market — for air-defense integration that does not require buying a single vendor's stack. That is a direct challenge to the closed, bundled air-defense architectures traditional primes sell.

bottomLine: Greece's up-to-$4 billion FMS package and Raytheon's up-to-$6.3 billion SM-3 multi-year deal show the two ends of the same pipeline: allies converting new NATO spending targets into US-sourced capability, and the US industrial base trying to turn framework agreements into real production. Simultaneously, a congressional report nearly doubling the Iran-war aircraft damage tally to 81 airframes worth up to $3.3 billion is the clearest sign yet of the attrition bill this war is running up. Meanwhile South Korea's first domestic hypersonic glide test and Britain's debate over overseas-versus-domestic spending both point the same direction: allies increasingly want indigenous capability and control, not just purchases from someone else's supply chain.
sources: Reuters, Breaking Defense, MarketWatch, The Hill, IBTimes Singapore, Sedaily, Yonhap/Operativ, The Guardian (Transition Security Project), Japan Times, Firstpost, Army Recognition, Forbes, MSN/CBS
